Born on March 22, 1958, in Wheeling, West Virginia, Kelley was the daughter of the late Jon Morton Burgess and Esther Louise (Gatchel) Lianna. She spent her early years in West Virginia before making Ohio her home, where she built a life rooted in faith, family, and cherished friendships. Kelley was a graduate of Salem High School and enjoyed a long career as a payroll specialist at The Vindicator. She was a former member of the Mill Creek Chapter of the American Business Women's Association. She was also an active member of Heritage Presbyterian Church, where she faithfully served as a deacon. Kelley loved working on puzzles, playing card games with family and friends, reading, and searching for treasures at auctions and yard sales. She was a devoted Steelers and Pirates fan, loved all things Disney, and enjoyed traveling with her beloved husband, Larry. Their favorite destinations included Las Vegas, North Carolina, and Niagara Falls, where they honeymooned. Kelley will be remembered for her genuine kindness and generous heart. She had a remarkable gift for making others feel welcome, and her warmth and thoughtfulness left a lasting impression on all who had the privilege of knowing her. In addition to her parents, Kelley was preceded in death by her cousin, Jim Pokas. She is survived by her husband, Lawrence Kurtz; her three sisters, Marjorie (George) Cadwallader, Jackie (Warren) Reis, and Amy (John) Bogaski; her aunt, Betty (the late Calvin) Pokas; her cousins, Dave Gatchel, Barbara (the late Donald) Warren, Judy (Duane) Mayles, John (Jane) Pokas, and Liz Stamp; her sisters-in-law, Nancy Kurtz and Arvona Miller; her brother-in-law, Martin (the late Josephine) Kurtz III; her nieces and nephews; her life-long friend, Marsha Arfman; and many extended family members and dear friends who will cherish her memory. Family and friends are invited to celebrate Kelley's life at a memorial service on Saturday, Aug. 15, 2026, at Heritage Presbyterian Church in Poland, Ohio. Cremation was private. Friends may visit with the family from 10 to 11 a.m., with the memorial service beginning at 11 a.m. A luncheon will follow the service. 8/12/26 Starting at /week. Subscribe Today

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: People gather during an Alternative for Germany (AfD) campaign rally ahead of Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters View image in fullscreen People gather during an Alternative for Germany (AfD) campaign rally ahead of Germany's Saxony-Anhalt state election on 6 September Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/Reuters Opinion Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) My home state is set to hand a breakthrough to the German far right. It’s a disaster decades in the making Marcus Böick A sense of abandonment could make Saxony-Anhalt the first state government to be solely led by the AfD. But the party’s hollow promises will only make a dire situation worse Thu 27 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share I t was in the summer of 2004 that I stopped understanding my own people. I was standing on a sweltering market square in Aschersleben, the town where I was born, picturesquely situated on the northern edge of the Harz mountains. A large crowd of angry people had gathered in front of a stage to protest about the welfare reforms (or, as many saw them, welfare cuts) introduced by the Social Democratic-Green coalition government under chancellor Gerhard Schröder. They chanted “We are the people!”, waved handpainted placards and seemed utterly beside themselves. I had gone to secondary school nearby, volunteered at the local hospital and interned at the local newspaper: I knew this place. And yet I found myself bewildered. What, exactly, did these deeply aggrieved people want – standing on a freshly renovated, almost idyllic market square? Weren’t things going reasonably well for them? Where did this burning resentment toward the west come from? Wasn’t the east-west divide supposed to be disappearing by now? More than two decades later, similar questions can once again be asked. Eastern Germany is facing a blue wave – or rather, a blue flood. In the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on 6 September, the far right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), whose party colour is blue, is almost certain to emerge as the largest party . Opinion polls consistently place the AfD above 40% , while the governing Christian Democrats (CDU) trail on around 23%. The Left party, once dominant in the east, has fallen to just 13%, while the Social Democrats (SPD) are struggling to clear the 5% electoral threshold. Should only three or four parties enter parliament, the way would be open for Germany’s first-ever state government led solely by the AfD. The established parties would find themselves stranded on the other side of the much-invoked political “ firewall ” against cooperation with the far right – and, for the first time since 1945, a party containing openly extremist factions would hold governmental power in a German federal state. The AfD would exercise considerable authority over policing, the judiciary, education and cultural affairs – areas that the party seeks fundamentally to “re-nationalise”, for example by reducing funding for memorial sites commemorating Nazi crimes and revising school curriculums to place greater emphasis on what it regards as the achievements of German history. For me – and, I suspect, for many East Germans who have left their homeland – the rise of these developments did not come as such a surprise. During my infrequent visits home over the past 10 years, it was palpable that something fundamental was shifting. When we celebrated the milestone birthday of an old school friend in early 2024, a group of longtime friends flew in to spend a cold January weekend together in Hettstedt. Yet while we cheerfully reminisced about old times, the friend’s family, whom I had always remembered as lively and eager to debate, just sat by, saying almost nothing. I was perplexed. Only later was I told that my friend’s mother – the heart of the family – had forbidden any political discussion. She feared that the guests who had come from afar would be deeply unsettled by how openly people now voiced views that had once been considered taboo. Saxony-Anhalt has always been a state with a difficult identity. In spite of an extraordinary cultural heritage – it is the home of Martin Luther, George Frideric Händel, Friedrich Nietzsche and the Bauhaus – it lacks a clearly defined regional character. Assembled from various territories of Prussia after its dissolution in 1947, it was abolished during the socialist German Democratic Republic and then re-established after reunification in 1990. Home to almost 3 million inhabitants at the time, Saxony-Anhalt entered the new era with tremendous optimism – only to suffer a brutal crash landing in the spring of 1991. East Germany’s state-owned industries were to be rapidly privatised by the Treuhand agency in an attempt to make them competitive in a market economy. Yet after decades of central planning and chronic shortages, the socialist combines were scarcely capable of surviving the massive shock produced by the economic and monetary union. Instead of the “flourishing landscapes” that chancellor Helmut Kohl had boldly promised, the whole region entered an unprecedented downward spiral. The metalworking and chemical industries of southern Saxony-Anhalt were hit particularly hard. During the spring of 1991, hundreds of thousands lost their jobs. Over the rest of the decade, many areas outside the main cities experienced industrial dismantling, mass unemployment and large-scale outmigration. Younger people, particularly well qualified women, began leaving the region. For my own generation, graduating around the turn of the millennium, moving away appeared to be the only viable path. At the same time, the state steadily withdrew from shrinking rural areas, closing schools and hospitals, relocating courts and police stations. Even the democratic political parties, always much less firmly rooted in eastern than in western Germany, became increasingly invisible. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The echoes of these immense transformations have grown louder once again over the past 35 years. On average, East Germans remain considerably poorer than their western counterparts. They possess significantly less wealth, inherit much less and often face markedly weaker career prospects. A lingering feeling of being “second-class citizens” has become deeply entrenched, extending even to generations born long after German reunification. I can understand these feelings, and I can understand how the AfD has channelled this pervasive sense of abandonment: through social media , local WhatsApp groups, football clubs and neighbourhood pubs. The anger no longer gathers helplessly on the town square; instead, it has found new energy and vastly greater reach in the digital sphere. And in the polling stations. What I can’t understand is that the people I grew up among are failing to see how hollow the AfD’s promises are. The slogans this party offers are not solutions. Many of the measures it advocates would only make a grim situation worse. How are businesses or hospitals supposed to recruit the skilled workers they urgently need if the main party simultaneously calls for large-scale “ remigration ”? How can anyone develop a positive vision of the future while at the same time expressing admiration for the Nazi reich or the GDR? It seems a case of suicide out of fear of death, as Bismarck is supposed to have said. Whether on a sun-drenched market square in the summer of 2004 or at a wintry family celebration in 2024, one thing became unmistakably clear to me: there are neither simple answers nor quick solutions. In Saxony-Anhalt, as elsewhere, the task will be to give people with sometimes very different views and values a genuine sense that they are being included on a shared path toward a common future. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Emergency services have responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Norwest, in Sydney’s north-west. Photograph: Ronnie Amini/AAP View image in fullscreen Emergency services have responded to reports of a shooting at a home in Norwest, in Sydney’s north-west. Photograph: Ronnie Amini/AAP Sydney Boy, 11, in serious condition after being shot in face and neck in Sydney home Three 18-year-old men were arrested at the unit in Norwest, police said, but officers played down link to organised crime Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Achol Arok and Catie McLeod Mon 21 Sep 2026 11.55 BST First published on Mon 21 Sep 2026 09.49 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An 11-year-old boy has been taken to hospital in a serious condition after being shot in a home in Sydney’s north-west. The child was receiving life-saving treatment in hospital on Monday night after suffering gunshot wounds to his face and neck, police said. He was found injured at about 5pm at a unit on Fairway Drive, Norwest, after emergency services arrived in response to reports of a shooting at the property. Paramedics treated the boy at the scene before taking him to hospital. Initial reports indicated the shots were fired from within the home. Speaking a few hours after the incident, Supt Naomi Moore said four 18-year-old men and a 44-year-old woman had been inside the unit at the time, all of whom were unharmed and were assisting with the investigation. Three of the 18-year-olds had been arrested, Moore said. Moore said while the investigation was just starting, police had no information to suggest the incident was related to organised crime. There have been at least six suspected mistaken-identity shootings in Sydney since the start of last year. Last week, two teenage boys were charged with murder after the recent shooting death of a university student in Sydney, which police say was a case of mistaken identity. Moore assured people in the community who were “fearful on the streets at the moment” that police did not believe Monday’s shooting in Norwood was related to organised crime. Police were investigating how the gun came to be in the house, as there were no firearms registered to that address, she said. Moore said she was not sure what type of gun had been used, or where the weapon was located. “In terms of what happened in that apartment, it is far too early for me to say right now,” she said. “[But] we have all sorts of resources down there … to ensure that we do get to the bottom of what happened in that unit tonight.” Police had established an “expansive” crime scene as investigations into the incident continued. “It’s a tragic situation with an 11-year-old child suffering this injury,” Moore said. “The mother is with the child at the moment – she is as distressed as any parent would be about what she is dealing with at the moment.” Explore more on these topics Sydney New South Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Beállítom Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök pénteken bejelentette, hogy kölcsönös látogatásokat szerveznek Magyar Péter miniszterelnökkel. „A találkozók pontos időpontjait a két ország illetékes csapatai egyeztetik majd” – írta közösségi oldalán az ukrán elnök, miután négyszemközt tárgyalt a magyar miniszterelnökkel Brüsszelben. Zelenszkij beszámolt arról, hogy a kétoldalú kapcsolatok legfontosabb kérdéseiről egyeztetett Magyar Péterrel, emellett pedig Ukrajna uniós csatlakozásának előrehaladását is megvitatták. Az ukrán elnök megköszönte a magyar miniszterelnöknek „az elvi alapokon nyugvó lépéseit”, és azt, hogy a magyar kormány hozzájárult ahhoz, hogy két új EU-csatlakozási klasztert megnyissanak Ukrajna számára. „Azon dolgozunk, hogy az év végéig megnyissuk a fennmaradó két klasztert is” – tette hozzá Zelenszkij. Az ukrán elnök szerint megvitatta Magyar Péterrel a diplomáciai helyzetet és az orosz–ukrán háború befejezésére irányuló erőfeszítéseket. Azt írta, hálás Magyar Péternek az Ukrajna és az ukrán nép iránt tanúsított szolidaritásáért, valamint azért, hogy kész együttműködni a béke megteremtése érdekében. „Szó esett az ukrán–magyar együttműködés lehetőségeiről, a kereskedelemről és a mezőgazdasági termékekkel kapcsolatos kérdésekről is” – tette hozzá Zelenszkij. Az ukrán elnök szerint Ukrajna mindig is a jószomszédi kapcsolatok és a kölcsönös megerősítés híve volt. „Megállapodtunk abban, hogy különböző szinteken újraindítjuk a közös munkát, és kölcsönös látogatásokat szervezünk. A találkozók időpontjait a két ország illetékes csapatai egyeztetik majd” – zárta posztját Zelenszkij. Az ukrán elnök az uniós állam- és kormányfők csúcstalálkozóján vett részt a belga fővárosban. Zelenszkij egy pénteki sajtótájékoztatón bővebben is beszélt a találkozóiról. Arra a kérdésre, hogy hajlandó lenne-e Budapesten újra találkozni a magyar miniszterelnökkel, azt felelte, hogy nincs ellenére. „Budapest? Nem vagyok ellene” – válaszolta Zelenszkij, hozzátéve, nem az a fontos, hogy ki látogat el először a másikhoz, hanem az, hogy közeledjenek.
